The near bank rises into a bank of foxglove spires taller than the boats, pink and freckled, bees working them from the bottom up.
A fallen birch lies half across the water, its peeled bark curling in white ribbons, ferns growing along its length and a kingfisher sitting on the highest point.
A steep mossy cut on the outer bend, hung with hart's-tongue fern and dripping, one thin waterfall coming down it into a clear pool.
Banks of meadowsweet and purple loosestrife standing shoulder-high along both sides, the flower heads leaning right out over the current.
An old willow leaning so far out that its whole crown trails in the water, the current combing its leaves downstream in long green lines.
A gravel spit on the inside of the bend, crowded with yellow flag iris, a heron standing motionless at the far end of it.
A stone footbridge of one mossy slab, with harebells growing out of the cracks and a dormouse sitting in the middle watching the race pass under.
The bank behind is a wall of red dogwood stems, bare and glowing, with a drift of wood anemone at their feet.
A ruined mill wheel half-sunk at the edge, green with weed, water still turning it slowly, forget-me-nots massed around its hub.
A stand of alder whose roots arch clear of the bank like a row of little doorways, each one dark inside, one with a lamp lit in it.
Hazel catkins hanging in yellow curtains over the water and dusting the surface with pollen wherever the boats disturb it.
A steep rocky shore of grey boulders with sea-green lichen and wild thyme in the cracks, and thrift flowering pink between them.
A quiet backwater to one side, skinned over with duckweed and white water-lilies, a frog on the biggest pad ignoring the whole regatta.
The bank is a bracken slope turning bronze, with a single rowan heavy in red berries leaning over the water.
Clumps of teasel and thistle gone to seed along the shore, silver-headed and backlit, goldfinches working through them.
A sandy undercut bank riddled with sand-martin holes, birds going in and out of it fast and low over the boats.
A grove of silver birch standing right to the water on the far side, their trunks doubled cleanly in the still margin.
A tumble of apple trees gone wild at the water's edge, windfalls bobbing in the shallows and a wasp on every one of them.
The near shore is thick with comfrey and butterbur, leaves as broad as a boat, a family of moorhens threading through the stems.
A holloway comes down to a ford beside the course, its banks overgrown to a green tunnel, bluebells right to the waterline.
A dead oak on the bend, bare and pale, every branch holding a watching bird and one holding a small fae in scarlet with her legs crossed.
A bank of sphagnum and sundew with cotton-grass standing above it, the whole thing glowing acid-green in the light.
A little wooden landing stage on stilts, grey and lichened, with coils of grass rope on it and a hedgehog asleep in one coil.
Wild garlic in flower carpeting the whole slope in white stars under hazel, the smell of it almost visible in the air.
A cliff of dark wet rock on the outer bank, curtained with liverwort and maidenhair, jackdaws calling from a crack near the top.
A low peat bank cut sheer by old floods, its dark face threaded with white quartz veins and a dipper bobbing at the wet base.
Bulrushes massed in a dense stand on the inside bank, their brown velvet heads splitting open and releasing slow drifts of white fluff across the water.
The outer bend is a shelf of flat limestone, pale and smooth, with stonewort growing in the shallows and a grass snake gliding between the slabs.
Rosebay willowherb gone to seed covering the whole upper bank in smoke, the fibres catching light and lifting off in threads over the course.
A dense mat of watercress filling a side-channel, vivid and dark green, small brown trout holding in the cold current behind it.
Gorse in full flower on the slope above, so thick and close the yellow presses down almost to the boats, the smell of coconut warm on the air.
A mossy log-jam wedged across a side-channel, liverwort cushioning every surface, a dipper walking along the submerged face of the lowest trunk.
Crack willows pollarded long ago and now bursting with new growth, each massive stump crowned with a fountain of silver-green wands.
The far bank shelves gently into weed-beds of water-crowfoot in white flower, the current drawing the stems into long pale ribbons below the surface.
Rushes burned black to stubble in a wide patch, bright green new shoots already pushing through, a lapwing standing at the edge of the burn.
A stream coming in from the left side over a lip of root and stone, making a small constant sound entirely separate from the noise of the regatta.
The bankside grass is long and seed-heavy and completely silver with dew, every blade bent at the same angle toward the water.
Ivy covering the entire face of a steep bank in one unbroken sheet, deep-rooted and dark, a wren moving fast and low through its interior.
A wide shallow fan of silt at a bend, colonised by water-pepper and pale persicaria, a snipe standing in the open centre of it.
Elder in full blossom overhanging the water, plate-sized heads of cream flower reflected in the dark pool below and yellowing its surface with fallen petals.
A granite boulder sitting mid-channel, half above water, cushioned with orange and grey lichen, a wagtail running circuits around its dry crown.
Hornbeam on the steep bank behind, their ribbed trunks bone-pale in the shade, clusters of papery winged seeds hanging down over the waterline.
A thatch of old reed-beds, brown and broken, with new green spears coming through at the base and a sedge warbler singing from deep inside.
The near bank slides into a reedmace colony, leaves upright and close as organ pipes, a coot's nest wedged between them at the waterline.
Dog roses scrambling out along the willow branches over the water, pale pink and paper-thin, the petals dropping into the current one at a time.
A bluff of red sandstone on the outer bank, warm and crumbling at the edges, ferns fingering out of every horizontal crack along its face.
Ash keys hanging in dense bunches from the trees above the right bank, dark and papery, spinning down onto the water in every current of air.
A shoal of small fish packed into the shadow under the start-bank overhang, their sides flashing silver in formation each time a hull passes over.
Blackthorn thicket growing right to the water, white blossom out before any leaves, the reflection of it making the margin look frosted.
A patch of flag-iris gone over, the orange and black seed-pods split and open along the near bank, seeds bright on the surface of the shallows.
A low peat bank cut sheer to the water, its dark layers striped like cake, ragged robin growing along the top edge in a loose pink fringe.
Clumps of rush and soft-grass half-submerged at the margins, sparkling with trapped air bubbles, a dragonfly hunting low between the stems.
The far shore shelves into a wide shingle bar pale as bone, ringed plover stepping along it quickly, each one leaving a tiny chain of prints.
A tangle of old bramble arching right out over the current, red-stalked and heavy with green unripe fruit, a yellowhammer perched at the furthest tip.
Bog myrtle crowding the near bank to the waterline, its small leaves bronze and aromatic, the crushed scent of it drifting across the whole reach.
A chunk of sandstone fallen from the bank above jutting into the shallows, covered in orange and grey rosette lichen, a newt resting flat on its top face.
Great horsetail standing in a dense column along the inside bend, jointed and prehistoric-looking, pale green, reaching well above the boats passing through.
A wet flush running down the bank face in a dark stain, watercress thick and bright in the trickle at its foot, the leaves trembling.
The outer bank rises into a clay overhang, swallow-tailed with old cracks, spotted orchids growing from the ledge along its whole length.
A beaver dam closing off a side channel, a smooth dome of stripped pale timber rising above the reeds, the pond behind it perfectly mirror-flat.
Pendulous sedge hanging in long arched sprays over the water, its fat spikelets swinging with each boat's wash, catching the light like green beads.
A thin spit of black mud jutting out on the inner bend, tracked all over with heron and coot prints, a water rail standing still at its tip.
A gnarled hawthorn leaning over the water with one low branch trailing, its bark corky and ridged, lichen-scabbed, a cluster of red haws weighing its tip down.
Reed canary grass making a wall twice the height of the racers along the straight, cream-flowered at the top, its base hidden in dark shadow.
A natural pool in the bank where a tree has tipped out, the crater full of rainwater and sphagnum, two mallards sitting in it ignoring the course.
The margin thick with flowering watercress spilling white into the stream, a water vole cutting through it and leaving a clean dark channel behind.
A long reach of chalk-white marl exposed on the bed in the shallows, the water above it impossibly clear, watercrowfoot waving in pale streamers.
Solomon's seal arching out from under the bank in a long curving row, its paired leaves holding tiny drops from the last rain still.
A stand of crack willow pollards along the bank, their swollen heads sprouting long new shoots in every direction, a kestrel still on the tallest one.
Ivy covering the whole face of a stone wall that runs down to the water, flowering ivy in round yellow-green clusters, red admiral butterflies all over it.
A mossy spring emerging at the foot of the bank, forming a pool the size of a hat before overflowing into the main channel, bright green and cold.
The bank flattens to a rough meadow right to the water's edge, yellow rattle and ox-eye daisy thick in it, bumblebees working it in every direction.
A wooden post rotten to a stump at the water's edge, lichen-covered and listing, meadow crane's-bill flowering purple around its base in a dense ring.
A floating island of consolidated reed and rush cut loose from the bank, drifting slowly broadside across the reach, a reed bunting clinging to its far edge.
Sweet cicely tall and white-flowered on the shaded bank, its fernlike leaves anise-scented, the hollow stems of last year's crop still standing pale between.
A reed bed filling the whole inner curve, the stems close-packed and rattling, a bittern frozen upright among them perfectly matching the verticals.
Bog myrtle low along the waterline, leaves dark and glossy, the crushed-spice smell of it reaching the boats as they pass close to the bank.
A clump of giant horsetail standing stiff as green candles at the margin, each segment ringed and precise, a damselfly on every topmost whorl.
The far bank undercut and rootbound, a curtain of ivy tumbling over the lip of it down to the water in one unbroken dark-green fall.
Pale wood sorrel covering the whole shaded slope in small trembling hearts, a great spotted woodpecker working the beech trunk at the top.
A cluster of mossy stones in the shallows, barely submerged, their tops dry and flat, a dipper walking between them against the current.
Guelder rose arching over the outer bank, the heavy white plates of its flowers just gone, berries beginning to form red in the green clusters.
A peat shelf at the bend, dark brown and crumbling at its lip, bog asphodel spiking yellow along the whole upper face of it.
Soft rush in tight round tufts covering a wide wet margin, and between the tufts a mat of marsh marigold still holding a few late blooms.
A gnarled hawthorn low and wind-bent over the water, its trunk pale grey and furrowed, a long grey beard of lichen swaying from every branch.
Water crowfoot in full white flower lying flat across a slow section, the blossoms packed so dense the surface underneath is barely visible.
An eroded clay bank on the outside of the turn, the layers red and cream and ochre striped, swallows skimming along its face.
A narrow channel between two islands of sedge, current quick and dark in it, a water vole sitting on a low ledge chewing something held in its paws.
Pennywort spangling the wet rock face in perfect round coins, bright green, each leaf holding a drop of water at its centre.
A stand of bulrush with brown velvet heads above the green, the heads splitting open to spill white floss that drifts across the course.
The bank rises to a low cliff of sandstone blocks, warm orange, with wallflowers seeded into every joint and a kestrel perched on the top edge.
Hemlock water-dropwort in white umbels banking the channel on both sides, tall and lush, the whole corridor smelling green and sharp.
A mat of floating pondweed pressed to the still margin, its leaves rust-brown at the edge, a moorhen pulling at the trailing roots from below.
Elder in heavy cream flower overhanging the water, the flat-topped heads reflecting below them so each cluster appears twice in the dark surface.
A row of pollarded willows along the far bank, knuckled and thick, each one with a spray of fresh silver shoots from the crown.
Cranesbill in dense violet patches along the top of the bank above the root line, bees moving through them in a low unhurried cloud.
Stepping stones crossing a shallow rapid at an angle to the course, each stone cushioned in orange and olive moss on its upstream face.
A spread of marsh thistle running purple down to the very edge of the water, brown marsh fritillaries resting on the open heads.
Otter prints in the soft mud at the ford crossing, fresh and clear, a smear of wet beside them where the animal came ashore.
A granite shelf sloping into the water at a long low angle, its surface pale and clean, wood anemone banked all along the upper edge of it.
